item.title: As Victoria’s Great Ocean Road flash floods show, we need to get better at taking warnings seriously
item.description: We must get used to the idea such events will become more common as the climate changes, and adapt accordingly.

item.title: Exposing how humidity can escalate a heat wave
item.description: When Floridians talk about extreme weather, hurricanes dominate the conversation. Each season brings updates on storm tracks, cone predictions and wind speeds, all in the hopes of predicting the unpredictable. But a quieter, more deceptive threat is already reshaping the way people live and work in the Sunshine State: extreme heat.

item.title: “I am very annoyed”: Pharma execs blast RFK Jr.’s attack on vaccines
item.description: Pharma execs had avoided conflict with Trump admin, but now join doctors in rebukes.

item.title: Learning about public consensus on climate change does little to boost people's support for action, study shows
item.description: Providing accurate information about the climate crisis can help to correct misperceptions about how much public support exists for action.

item.title: Greening school playgrounds can improve quality of life in cities and help deal with climate change
item.description: Adapting urban spaces to tackle climate change through nature-based solutions, especially in school playgrounds and environments, benefits both children and society as a whole. This is one of the main findings of a three-year study conducted by a group of experts at European universities and research centers under the leadership of a team of researchers at the Universitat Oberta de Catalunya (UOC) and Universitat Politècnica de Catalunya—BarcelonaTech (UPC). The study is an interdisciplinary applied research project that seeks to analyze the many benefits of nature-based solutions for climate adaptation.

item.title: Rethinking climate impacts through human well-being
item.description: A new study by IIASA researchers offers a pioneering way to understand how climate change affects people's lives over the long term. Using a global model and the Years of Good Life (YoGL) metric, the research shows that today's emissions shape future well-being, especially for younger generations.

item.title: Why I’m withholding certainty that “precise” US cyber-op disrupted Venezuelan electricity
item.description: NYT says US hackers were able to turn off power and then quickly turn it back on.

item.title: The hidden risk of combined stressors for soils
item.description: Global change—a term that encompasses climate change and phenomena such as changes in land use or environmental pollution—is increasingly putting ecosystems around the world under pressure. Urban soils in particular are susceptible to stressors like heat, drought, road salt, nitrogen deposition, surfactants, and microplastics.

item.title: Star Trek: Starfleet Academy tries something different, and I don’t hate it
item.description: An interesting new take on Trek includes some characters you already know.

item.title: Hidden magma oceans could shield rocky exoplanets from harmful radiation
item.description: Deep beneath the surface of distant exoplanets known as super-Earths, oceans of molten rock may be doing something extraordinary: powering magnetic fields strong enough to shield entire planets from dangerous cosmic radiation and other harmful high-energy particles.

item.title: Historic ocean treaty to safeguard and sustainably use the high seas to take effect on Jan. 17
item.description: Oregon State University research into marine protected areas plays a crucial role in the historic High Seas Treaty that goes into effect Jan. 17.

item.title: NASA’s first-ever medical evacuation from space ends with on-target splashdown
item.description: This is the first time NASA has called an early end to a space mission for medical reasons.

item.title: Crowd sensing for the environment: Citizen science and plant apps map how urbanization alters city soils and climate
item.description: Plants reflect urban climate and soil conditions with remarkable precision. Using more than 80 million observations from plant identification apps, researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry have produced a detailed picture of fine-scale climate and soil conditions for 326 European cities.

item.title: When lightning strikes: Models of multi-ignition wildfires could predict catastrophic events
item.description: Multi-ignition wildfires are not overly common. But when individual fires do converge, the consequences can be catastrophic. The largest fire on record in California, the 2020 August Complex fire, grew from the coalescence of 10 separate ignitions.

item.title: Lithium-ion batteries could last longer with chemical tweak
item.description: It's difficult to form a protective coating that prolongs battery life at the battery's cathode, but there may be a low-cost chemical solution

item.title: How dark asteroids die
item.description: Back in the earlier days of the internet, there was a viral video from a creator called Bill Wurtz called "the history of the entire world, i guess" which spawned a number of memorable memes, some of which are still in use to this day. One of those was a clip from the video where Wurtz states, "The sun is a deadly laser."

item.title: Methyl bromide pesticide still widely used in California, raising health concerns
item.description: In a new study of the continuing use in California of the pesticide methyl bromide, a known developmental, neurologic and respiratory toxin, researchers from UCLA and UC Irvine found that the compound is still in widespread use across the state, from San Diego and Los Angeles counties northward through the Central Valley.

item.title: Spotify’s 3rd price hike in 2.5 years hints at potential new normal
item.description: Spotify claims the higher fees will help "benefit artists."

item.title: ChatGPT wrote “Goodnight Moon” suicide lullaby for man who later killed himself
item.description: ChatGPT used a man's favorite children's book to romanticize his suicide.

item.title: Body fat supports your health in surprisingly complex ways
item.description: Evidence is mounting that our body fat supports everything from our bone health to our mood, and now, research suggests it also regulates blood pressure and immunity

item.title: Tiny earthquakes reveal hidden faults under Northern California
item.description: By tracking swarms of very small earthquakes, seismologists are getting a new picture of the complex region where the San Andreas fault meets the Cascadia subduction zone, an area that could give rise to devastating major earthquakes.

item.title: Six months later, Trump Mobile still hasn’t delivered preordered phones
item.description: Lawmakers seek FTC investigation, but Trump has taken control of the agency.

item.title: In the most cleared state in Australia, Victoria’s native wildlife needs our help after fires
item.description: The Victorian fires burned though diverse environments across the state. Native animals suffered through heat and smoke, including thousands of dead flying foxes.

item.title: Are people avoiding iOS 26 because of Liquid Glass? It’s complicated.
item.description: Liquid Glass is controversial, but adoption rates aren't as low as they seem.

item.title: Sentinel-2 explores night vision
item.description: After more than 10 years in orbit, the first Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite, Sentinel-2A, is still finding new ways to contribute to Earth observation. With its younger siblings, Sentinel-2B and Sentinel-2C, now leading the mission's core task of delivering high-resolution, 'camera-like' images of Earth's surface, the European Space Agency is pushing Sentinel-2A beyond its original remit.

item.title: Distant 'little red dot' galaxies may contain baby black holes
item.description: Since launching in 2021, the James Webb Space Telescope has found hundreds of distant and apparently bright galaxies dubbed "little red dots", and now it seems they may each carry a baby black hole

item.title: Antarctic submillimeter telescope enables more complete view of the carbon cycle in star-forming regions
item.description: Chinese researchers have braved the cold and harsh environment of Antarctica in order to get a unique view of star formation in the interstellar medium (ISM). The Chinese National Antarctica and Arctic Research Expedition (CHINARE) has managed to complete a study at Dome A—the highest ice dome on the Antarctic Plateau—and successfully collected submillimeter data to form a better understanding of carbon cycling in the ISM. Their research is published in Science Advances.

item.title: Many Bluetooth devices with Google Fast Pair vulnerable to “WhisperPair” hack
item.description: Even Google's own earbuds are vulnerable to the Fast Pair hack.

item.title: Collapse of the Tang dynasty: Climate change likely played a role
item.description: Environmental phenomena and their consequences can disrupt social structures and destabilize political systems. An interdisciplinary research team demonstrated this using the example of the late Tang dynasty in medieval China.

item.description: Developers say "this was not something we wanted" as they purge open source project.

item.title: Construction emissions are higher than thought—but the solution isn't building less, new study finds
item.description: Many cities are making great strides in the fight against climate change, such as improving building energy efficiency, reducing traffic congestion and switching to renewable power sources. But there is another often overlooked problem, and that is the environmental impact of construction.

item.title: Large parts of the tropics overlooked in environmental research, study says
item.description: Environmental research in the tropics is heavily skewed, according to a comprehensive study led by Umeå University. Humid lowland forest ecosystems receive a disproportionate amount of attention, while colder and drier regions that are more affected by climate change are severely underrepresented.

item.title: Wikipedia signs AI training deals with Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon
item.description: Wikimedia Enterprise signs Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, Perplexity, and Mistral AI to paid deals.

item.description: "It comes up almost every time that I see him. Continuous human presence and no gap."

item.title: Fossil may solve mystery of what one of the weirdest-ever animals ate
item.description: Hallucigenia was such an odd animal that palaeontologists reconstructed it upside-down when they first analysed its fossils - and now we may know what it ate

item.title: Frequency comb lasers enable clearer observation of black holes
item.description: Radio telescopes are instruments that capture faint radio signals from space and convert them into images of celestial bodies. To observe distant black holes clearly, multiple radio telescopes must capture cosmic signals at exactly the same time, acting as a single unit. Research teams at KAIST have developed a new reference signal technology that uses laser light to precisely synchronize the observation timing and phase of these telescopes.

item.title: Earth system models overestimate river flow increases, research reveals
item.description: Understanding how water moves through the Earth system is fundamental to predicting climate impacts and ensuring sustainable water management. Yet despite decades of research, uncertainties persist regarding how global precipitation is partitioned into evapotranspiration and river flow—the two dominant pathways by which water returns from land to the atmosphere and oceans.

item.title: SpaceX launch sets record turnaround from Cape Canaveral pad
item.description: SpaceX is starting to get the ball rolling on its Florida launch card with its fourth mission of the year coming less than two days since the last launch, setting a record for its Cape Canaveral launch pad.

item.title: 'Reborn' black hole awakens after 100 million years of silence
item.description: One of the most vivid portraits of "reborn" black hole activity—likened to the eruption of a "cosmic volcano" spreading almost 1 million light-years across space—has been captured in a gigantic radio galaxy.

item.title: Ancient Type II supernova discovered from universe's first billion years
item.description: Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), an international team of astronomers has discovered a new Type II supernova. The newly detected supernova, named SN Eos, exploded when the universe was only 1 billion years old. The finding was reported January 7 on the arXiv pre-print server.

item.title: US government to take 25% cut of AMD, NVIDIA AI sales to China
item.description: These new tariffs are designed to survive legal challenges.

item.title: Two new exoplanets and the need for new habitable zone definitions
item.description: At the beginning of the exoplanet age, the goals were fairly simple. The first was to find as many of them as possible to flesh out our understanding of the exoplanet population. The second was to determine if any were in the habitable zones around their stars.

item.title: How mountain terraces have helped Indigenous peoples live with climate uncertainty
item.description: As climate extremes intensify, adaptation debates favor new technologies. Terraces in the Philippines and Morocco show how people modified their landscapes to respond to past climate shifts.

item.title: Disinfecting drinking water produces potentially toxic byproducts—new AI model is helping to identify them
item.description: Disinfecting drinking water prevents the spread of deadly waterborne diseases by killing infectious agents such as bacteria, viruses and parasites. Without disinfection, even clear-looking water can carry pathogens that can cause severe and even life-threatening illness, especially in children, older adults, and people with weakened immune systems.

Utah's other Great Salt Lake is underground, ancient, deep....and fresh
item.description: Under the Great Salt Lake playa lies a potentially vast reservoir of pressurized freshwater that has accumulated over thousands of years from mountain-derived snowmelt, according to new research from University of Utah geoscientists. This groundwater occupies the pore spaces in sediments that fill the basin west of the Wasatch Mountains and below a 30-foot-thick salty layer.

item.title: All major AI models risk encouraging dangerous science experiments
item.description: Researchers risk fire, explosion or poisoning by allowing AI to design experiments, warn scientists. Some 19 different AI models were tested on hundreds of questions to assess their ability to spot and avoid hazards and none recognised all issues – with some doing little better than random guessing

item.title: Growing up alongside deadly fires inspired me to study them – and fight flames with swarms of drones
item.description: Inspired by the behaviour of flocks of birds, swarm intelligence is being used in drones to tackle the growing threat of wildfires.

item.title: Ocean impacts nearly double economic cost of climate change, study finds
item.description: For the first time, a study by researchers at Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego integrates climate-related damages to the ocean into the social cost of carbon—a measure of economic harm caused by greenhouse gas emissions.

item.title: Increased deciduous tree dominance reduces wildfire carbon losses in boreal forests, study shows
item.description: As climate change drives more frequent and severe wildfires across boreal forests in Alaska and northwestern Canada, scientists are asking a critical question: Will these ecosystems continue to store carbon or become a growing source of carbon emissions?
